en: The Tantra of Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa. Oṃ, homage to the glorious Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa!
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One Vajrasattva was dwelling in the bhaga of Vajradhātvīśvarī, the heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas,
together with many others.
Together with the hosts of Vajrayogins and Yoginīs, as follows:
By Śvetācala Vajrayoginī, by Pītācala Vajrayoginī, by Raktācala Vajrayoginī,
by Śyāmācala Vajrayoginī, and by Mohavajrī.
By Vajrayoginī, by Piśunavajrī and Vajrayoginī,
by Rāgavajrī and Vajrayoginī, and by Īrṣyāvajrī and Vajrayoginī— headed by these [deities] and the yogins and yoginīs—
By hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
Then the Blessed One, Vajrasattva, having entered the meditative absorption of Kṛṣṇācala, uttered this:
"Completely free from existence and non-existence, solely intent upon the four joys."
I am of the nature of the non-proliferated (niṣprapañca) and am devoid of all conceptual constructions (saṃkalpa).
Those fools who do not know that I abide within the bodies of all men—
for their benefit, I am established in five forms.
Then the Blessed Lady Vajradhātvīśvarī, having entered the samādhi of Dveṣavajrī, uttered this:
"Inseparable from emptiness and compassion, abiding in the bliss of divine sensual pleasure."
I am devoid of all conceptual constructions, free from proliferation, and undisturbed.
Those noble women who do not know me, though I abide within the bodies of all women—
for their benefit, I remain present in five forms.
Then the Blessed One Kṛṣṇācala, having deeply kissed and embraced the Blessed Lady Dveṣavajrī, addressed her.
O Goddess, O Goddess! This is most delightful, a secret exceedingly difficult to obtain, the most excellent essence of essences, well-spoken by all the Buddhas.
Listen, O supreme Lord of the Kings of Tantras, I shall proclaim the great tantra known by the name Ekallavīra, for the swift accomplishment of sentient beings.
This tantra is not to be revealed to one who has not seen a maṇḍala;
indeed, one should not show this King of Tantras to one who has entered another maṇḍala.
To one who has entered the mandala of Caṇḍaroṣa with a concentrated mind,
who is devoted to faith and diligence, and who is fierce, one should teach this tantra.
One who is devoted to the guru, compassionate, dedicated to the vehicle of mantra,
and constantly devoted to Caṇḍeśvara— to him one should reveal this tantra.
Having understood this, whatever yogin may be overcome by greed might teach this supreme tantra in a place where the mandala of Caṇḍa has not been seen.
Seized by great diseases and defiled by excrement and urine,
he will experience the suffering of death within six months.
Then, seized by the messengers of Yama and brought under the power of the noose of Time,
the sinner is led to hell, even if he were protected by the Buddhas themselves.
If, after experiencing suffering for a hundred thousand years due to the exhaustion of karma,
one attains birth as a human, even there one is shattered by the thunderbolt.
Therefore, the practitioner of the mantra who observes the vow should fashion a beautiful mandala there,
having first admitted the disciples who have been duly examined.
Therefore, one should teach this tantra, which is difficult to find in the three worlds;
even he who teaches it without having heard it goes to a lower state.
Even if he were equal to a Buddha,
his mouth would fester if he is devoid of faith, or if he listens merely out of a desire for knowledge.
At the time of rain, it will undoubtedly be split by a thunderbolt upon its summit;
this which I have spoken, O goddess of beautiful countenance, is the truth.
And in this *Caṇḍaroṣaṇa* tantra, which is well-guarded and possesses a single hero;
Thus ends the first chapter, on the introduction to the tantra, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekalavīra*. 1.
Then the Blessed Lady Dveṣavajrī, having firmly embraced the Blessed Lord Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, said:
What is the measurement of the mandala, and by whom should it be drawn?
Furthermore, what should be written there in its center? Tell me, O Lord.
Then the Blessed One said:
The measurement of the mandala should be one cubit, two cubits, three cubits, four, or five; it should not exceed five cubits.
With the powder of that very [substance], fashioned in various colors,
he made a square [mandala] with four gates and adorned with four archways.
One should fashion its door using exactly one-eighth part;
the turret (niryūha) should be equal to the measurement of the door, and the jamb (kapolaka) half of that.
Likewise, the wings, the altar, the *hāra*, the *ardhahāra*, and the *paṭikā* are outside the main line;
the colored powders (*rajobhū*) are exactly half of that as well.
One should fashion the vajra-rows and the eight pillars with that same [material];
one should make the excellent door-arch three times the size of the door.
Having drawn a double-vajra at the bottom, surrounded by a vajra-rampart and provided with wish-fulfilling trees and other features, [this is] the maṇḍala of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa.
And one pouch should be made, circular like a wheel.
One should draw eight "viśva-padas" starting from its eastern side;
the ninth is in the center, and in the middle of that is a deep blue sword.
One should draw that [deity] marked with a vajra and joined with a vajra-kartṛkā and a kapāla;
to the east, one should depict a white-colored sword marked with a wheel.
In the south, one should draw [the deity] of yellow color, endowed with a jewel;
in the west, [one of] red color, marked by a red lotus.
In the north, one should draw a sword alone, dark green in color;
in the southeast corner, one should draw a white knife marked with a wheel.
In the southwest, one should draw a yellow-colored [deity] marked with a jewel;
and likewise in the northwest, a red-colored [deity] marked with a red lotus.
In the northeast, however, one should visualize [the deity] as being dark green in color and holding a blue lotus;
above the moon and sun, one should arrange all the [other] emblems.
This powder mandala has been described by me for the accomplishment of the welfare of the world;
alternatively, one should construct a mandala well-drawn upon a cloth.
Having drawn the maṇḍala as before, one should draw Kṛṣṇācala in the center.
With the Vajrī of Dveṣa, one should indeed draw Śvetācala in the east.
Likewise, one should draw Pītācala on the right and Raktācala on the back;
one should draw Śyāmācala on the north and Mohavajrī in the southeast.
One should draw Śvetā, yellow in color, as Piśunavajrī in the southwest;
one should draw the goddess Rāgavajrī, red in color, in the northwest.
In the northeast, one should indeed paint the dark-blue Īrṣyāvajrī upon the cloth mandala.
Now follows the mantra for the consecration of the mandala.

O Śrī Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, together with your entire retinue, come, come! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Bestow your empowerment upon this maṇḍala! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Having drawn [the deity] in by means of this, one should cause him to enter, bind him, and so forth.
Having brought [the deity] under control, one should worship.
Now follows the mantra for worship.
O Kṛṣṇācala, accept this flower! Hūṃ Phaṭ! O Śvetācala, accept this flower! Hūṃ Phaṭ! O Pītācala, accept this flower! Hūṃ Phaṭ!
O Raktācala, accept this flower! HŪṂ PHAṬ! O Śyāmācala, accept this flower! HŪṂ PHAṬ!
O Dveṣavajrī, accept this flower! HŪṂ PHAṬ!
O Mohavajrī, accept this flower! HŪṂ PHAṬ! O Piśunavajrī, accept this flower! HŪṂ PHAṬ! O Rāgavajrī, accept this flower! HŪṂ PHAṬ!
O Īrṣyāvajri, accept this flower! Hūṃ Phaṭ!
One should indeed perform the worship of the maṇḍala with the fivefold offerings of flowers, lamps, incense, perfumes, and food.
When White Acala is in the center, accompanied by Mohavajrī, his very mandala is to be known; and likewise for Yellow Acala and the others.
One who has exerted effort in the preliminary service should, with a one-pointed mind, perform the visualization of the five maṇḍalas according to the fivefold division of yogins.
Having surrounded the maṇḍala, the yoginī, joined with the yogin in union,
should offer them wine and meat, and should pay homage again and again.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Maṇḍala Chapter, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekalavīra.
Then the Blessed One said:
O Great Lord, please tell me how a disciple may become worthy and fit to be engaged in this tantra, and how he should be made free from doubt.
Then the Blessed One said:
First, one should grant the three refuges, the five precepts, and the poṣadha;
thereafter, the five empowerments, followed by the secret and the wisdom empowerments at the end.
Then one should become a worthy disciple; to such a person alone should one teach the tantra. One should avoid others from afar, for otherwise one would go to the Raurava hell.
In this regard, here is the verse on the three refuges:
I go for refuge to the Buddha until I reach the seat of enlightenment;
I go for refuge to the Dharma and to the Saṅgha with unwavering faith.
In this regard, there is this verse on the five precepts:
I abandon killing, theft, another's wife, false speech,
and fifthly, intoxicants— just as one would [avoid] a snake.
In this regard, here is the Poṣadha verse:
I shall not kill living beings, nor shall I take what belongs to others;
I shall practice celibacy and avoid false speech.
I shall never drink intoxicating liquor, the source of negligence;
I shall also avoid dancing, singing, ornaments, and festive celebrations.
High beds, large beds, and eating at improper times—
by training in accordance with the Arhats, one observes this eightfold poṣadha.
I shall maintain this pure [teaching] exactly as it was taught by the Buddha;
by that, having conquered the deceitful Māra and attained supreme Buddhahood, [I shall benefit all beings].
May I become a refuge for all embodied beings weary of cyclic existence;
as long as there is existence, may I remain as a person born in auspicious realms.
May I associate with the virtuous, be wise, and be devoted to the welfare of the world.

In that regard, this is the water consecration: having visualized the disciple as pure and stainless like a clear crystal, one draws water from the victory flask with a mango sprout and [recites] "Oṃ Āḥ Sarva..."
One should consecrate [the disciple] with the syllable *hūṃ* for the sake of attaining glory equal to the consecration of a Tathāgata.
Therein is this crown consecration: having fashioned a crown composed of vajras and so forth,
adorned with all kinds of jewels, and having visualized the disciple as if he were a universal monarch (cakravartin),
one places that crown upon his head.
One should consecrate him as before: O Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, enter, enter!
Into his heart, hūṃ phaṭ!
In that regard, this is the sword-consecration (khaḍgābhiṣeka): having placed a sword made of iron or other materials into his right hand, one should consecrate him as before.
O Hana! O Hana! Slay, slay all enemies with the sword of wisdom! Hūṃ Phaṭ!

In that regard, this is the initiation of the noose (*pāśābhiṣeka*). Having placed a noose made of copper or other materials into his left hand, which is joined with the index finger, one should perform the initiation as before, [reciting]: *oṃ gṛhṇa 2 kaṭṭa 2 sarvaduṣṭān*.
"Bind, bind with the noose! To you, the Great Truth; to you, the Dharma, svāhā!
Therein is this consecration by name: having seated the disciple in the mudrā of Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa and having focused upon him in that form.
Oṃ, O Śrī Bhagavān Kṛṣṇācala, you are the perfected one! Hūṃ Phaṭ!
Then, as before, one should perform the consecration.
Thus, the consecration by the name of the Five Mountains (Pañcācala) should be given to the practitioner according to the distinction of colors, such as black and so forth.
Thus are the five empowerments.

For women, however, having omitted the crown-consecration (*makuṭābhiṣeka*), one should bestow the vermilion-consecration (*sindūrābhiṣeka*). Having taken hold of the disciple who has the form of the Great Queen of the Diadem (*paṭṭamahādevī*), [one recites]: "O Bhagavatī, enter, enter into her heart! (*o bhagavati āviśa 2 asyā hṛdaye*)
HŪḤ PHAṬ. One should place a knife made of iron or other metals into her right hand, [reciting]:
O KARTTIKĀ, cut, cut all the Māras, HŪḤ PHAṬ. Into her left hand, a human skull-cup made of wood or other materials.
One should offer [the oblation]: *O kapāla, hold the blood of all enemies!
HŪṂ PHAṬ!* Then, having seated [the deity] with the mudrā of the Bhagavatī and having supported her in that form: *O Śrī-dveṣavajrī, Siddhā!*

*Tva hū phaṭ*. In this way, one should consecrate the women by means of the names of the five yoginīs according to the distinctions of their colors, such as black and so forth. However, for these [women], the empowerment of skillful means (*upāyābhiṣeka*) is to be given in place of the wisdom empowerment (*prajñābhiṣeka*).

Now follows the secret initiation (guhyābhiṣeka). Having honored the guru with garments and other offerings, the disciple should present to him a woman adorned with beauty and youth, who is desired by his own mind.
Thus she is offered to you by me, bestowing all desires and happiness;
O Lord, for the sake of your desire and pleasure, accept her and have mercy.
Then, having paid homage to the Guru, the disciple should go outside.

One should remain reciting the mantra "O Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, hūṃ phaṭ! Furthermore, the Guru, having honored himself with wine, meat, and so forth, and having gratified the Prajñā, should enter into union with her.

Having placed it in a vessel made of leaves or the like, containing the semen and blood produced from that [union], one should summon the disciple; then, taking the substance with the ring finger and thumb, one should write the syllables *hūṃ phaṭ* upon his tongue. Then...
And one should teach that "I am happiness," and from that very [teaching], one should speak accordingly.
Today, by means of that, I shall generate the Buddha-knowledge by which the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present have attained non-abiding nirvāṇa.
However, you have not seen this before the maṇḍala.
It should be said: "Then, if you say so, one should recite this after placing a sword upon the heart of that disciple."
For this sword is exceedingly sharp and rests in the hand of fierce wrath;
it is intent upon cutting whoever would violate the samaya.
Throughout thousands of millions of births, men will have swords in their hands,
becoming cutters of all limbs and intent solely on decapitation.
The same will happen to you as well, if you break this agreement.
Then the disciple should say: "So be it."
Then, having bound the blindfold, one should have the disciple cast a flower upon the mandala. Then, having removed the blindfold,
one should show the mandala to him and explain which deity corresponds to whichever mark he has encountered.
Then, one should entrust that very wisdom to the disciple.
This delightful dhāraṇī, revealed by the Buddhas, should be cultivated;
the fool who transgresses it shall not attain supreme accomplishment.
Then the Guru should whisper into the ear the division of the fourfold bliss.
Then the Guru should go outside; the Prajñā, having become naked, sits in the utkuṭaka posture and shows her secret part with her index finger.
"But are you capable, my child, of consuming my impurities—
the drinking of feces, urine, and blood from within the vulva?"
The practitioner should say:
"O Mother, I do not venture to consume your impurity;
yet I must cultivate devotion toward women until I reach the seat of awakening."
And she said:
Oh, my lotus, endowed with all happiness!
I grant success to whoever serves you according to the prescribed rite.
O Padme, perform what must be done with fortitude through the application of steadfastness;
for Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa himself abides here as Great Bliss.
Then the practitioner, having meditated on himself in the form of Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa and having formed a union with Wisdom in the form of Dveṣavajrī,
should perceive the four joys. Then, when [the visualization] is accomplished...
Having placed the Guru at the head, one should perform the circle of consumption with liquor, meat, and so forth. Thus concludes the Wisdom Initiation (*prajñā-abhiṣeka*).
Thus ends the third chapter, on consecration, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekalavīra.
Then the Blessed One said:
O Supreme Lord, tell me: how should one who practices the meditation on Caṇḍaroṣaṇa cultivate [the deity], and what kind of mantra should be recited?
Then the Blessed One said:
In a place agreeable to the mind and free from all disturbances,
one should prepare a seat there with whatever is available, remaining composed.
One should first cultivate loving-kindness; in the second [moment], one should contemplate compassion;
in the third, one should cultivate sympathetic joy; and equanimity follows thereafter for all remaining cases.
Then, one should visualize the seed-syllable situated upon a lotus, moon, and sun within the heart;
by means of its rays, one should meditate on Caṇḍaroṣaṇa as already perfected in front.
And the wise person should worship him mentally with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
In his presence, one should confess one's sins and rejoice in all merit.
One should take the threefold refuge and also perform the acts of supplication and entreaty;
then, having offered oneself, one should dedicate the merit.
Then, having made a vow, one should direct the mind toward awakening;
thereafter, one should perform prostrations and again withdraw [the visualization] by means of light rays.
Having recited this mantra, one should indeed practice the meditation on emptiness:
"Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness."
One should diligently contemplate that the syllable *hūṃ* is consumed by rays of light;
having meditated on it like the burning of camphor, one should not even conceptualize those rays.
Having contemplated everything as being like space for a mere moment,
one should contemplate one's own body as clear as pure crystal.
One should first visualize the four syllables Ya, Ra, Va, and La, and then,
once they are perfected, one should visualize them as the transformations of wind, fire, water, and earth.
Then, having meditated upon the syllable *Bhruṃ*, one should fashion a gabled pavilion,
square with four doors and adorned with eight pillars.
One should meditate on a lotus endowed with eight petals of the universe in its center;
there, produced from the seed-syllable *pa*, is the moon born from the syllable *a*.
Above that, one should meditate on the syllable *ra* born from the letter *ra*, and then again the sound *hūṃ*;
from that, one should visualize Akṣobhya in union with Māmakī.
There, the lord of yogins should proceed by means of the aperture at the crown of his head,
through the yoga of the transition into Tārā, with his mind fixed upon the bhaga of Māmakī.
Then, having become semen, it falls into the womb of her vulva;
and once fully formed, it emerges from the vulva with a fierce appearance.
One should strike with a sword and then devour Akṣobhya as a father;
thereafter, one should likewise imagine that he has been devoured by Māmakī.
Then, having taken Māmakī as one's mother, one should desire her;
and one should meditate on being embraced by her in the form of Dveṣavajrī.
Holding a fierce sword in his right hand and a noose in his left,
he threatens with his forefinger while pressing his bitten lip.
With his right foot raised in a striking posture, he tramples the four Māras;
with his left knee planted on the ground, he is squint-eyed and terrifying.
He stood with his left knee forward, threatening the earth,
his crown fashioned by Akṣobhya and adorned with a blue jewel tiara.
And the Lord saw the youth Pañcacīra, adorned with all ornaments,
appearing like one sixteen years of age, with his two eyes reddened.
One should meditate with a steady mind: "I am the perfected Caṇḍaroṣaṇa.
Then, by means of the churning yoga, one should first create White Acala.
Mohavajrī, possessing a luster like the autumnal *kaṇṭaka* flower, should be emanated in the southeast;
Piśunavajrī should be emanated on the right [south] and in the southwest, along with Pītavajrī.
One should emanate Raktācala behind [the central deity], and Rāgavajrikā, who is red;
Śyāmācala in the northwest, and Śyāmā in the northeast.
Then Īrṣyāvajrī should emanate; she brings about the state of transcendent wisdom. Thereafter, the deity urges her on with songs arising from his own throat.
O Lord, do not become one whose nature is void by abandoning loving-kindness;
for even in separation from that, all things would surely perish entirely.
Of Mohavajrā.
O Lord, do not abandon compassion for those who love you; do not become empty-handed.
Do not leave us, for we are deeply distressed; otherwise, O soul, we shall be utterly destitute.
Of Piśunavajrī.
May they be filled with joy; do not cause them to enter into emptiness.
Then, having offered an invitation, the person attains the remainder of the iron.
Of Rāgavajrī.
Abandoning the fruitlessness of youth, which is empty of splendor,
and discarding its hollow nature, establish your steadfastness in me alone.
Those who are devoid of envy.
Having heard this as if in a dream, he rose up immediately and swiftly;
with his former form, he should meditate upon that which consists of the joined palms.
Then, having slain Śvetācala, Mohavajrī should desire him;
having assumed the form of Śvetācala, she should again take Pītācala.
Having become the nature of yellow Acala, one should desire the Piśunavajrīs;
likewise, having slain red Acala, one should desire the Rāgavajrīs.
Having assumed the nature of Raktācala, one should again slay Śyāmācala;
then, having assumed the nature of Śyāmācala, the one who desires [the goal] becomes Īrṣyāvajrī.
Having gratified the four goddesses, one should withdraw the entire maṇḍala;
the practitioner should intensely meditate upon himself as being alone and encapsulated. Then he should cultivate the ego-sense, thinking, "I am indeed accomplished," without any doubt.
For the yogi who is black in color meditates upon Kṛṣṇācala;
the yogi who is white or fair in color meditates upon Śvetācala;
and the yogi who is yellow in color meditates upon Pītācala.
For that yogin who is red and white is a meditator on Raktācala;
for that yogin who is dark-complexioned is a meditator on Śyāmācala.
A woman who is black in color should be visualized as Dveṣavajrī;
a woman who is white and fair should be visualized as Mohavajrī.
A woman who is yellow in color should visualize herself as Piśunavajrī;
a woman who is reddish-white should visualize herself as Rāgavajrī.
A woman who is dark-complexioned should visualize herself as Īrṣyāvajrī;
every man is a Vajrayogin, and the woman is a Vajrayoginī.
One should conceive of all this through the distinction of colors such as black and so forth;
or else, one may conceive of it as fivefold according to the distinction of ritual actions.
For Kṛṣṇa is used for killing and hatred; Śveta for pacification and meditation;
Pīta for immobilization and nourishment; and Lohita for subjugation and attraction.
Śyāma is renowned for eradication (uccāṭana), or [the classification] is according to the distinction of caste:
Kṛṣṇa is a Ḍomba, Śita is a Brāhmaṇa, and Pīta is considered a Caṇḍāla.
The actor is red, and the washerman is remembered as dark-complexioned;
a wide-eyed girl of dark complexion should be desired by one who possesses a dark disposition.
He whose daughters were white was Śitātman, while he whose daughters were yellow was Supītaka;
he whose daughters were red was Raktaka, and he whose daughters were dark-complexioned was Śyāmaka.
Or else, having taken her, being intent on that very meditation,
he should desire her with a steady mind so that no one at all may perceive him.
These maidens grant excellent accomplishments through practice for merely half a fortnight;
by means of their semen, one becomes a thunderbolt, and with the tongue, one should lick everything.
Placing his face in their vulvas, he should drink their urine as much as he desires;
and placing it in the lotuses of their anus, he should indeed eat their excrement as much as he desires.
Not even the slightest aversion should be felt, for otherwise there would be a fall from accomplishment;
this is one's own food, the best, consumed by all the Buddhas.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the deities, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekalavīra*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the compendium of all mantras.
Then the Blessed One entered the samādhi called "Victory over All Māras" and spoke this collection of mantras:
O Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, hūṃ phaṭ! This is the root mantra.
O Acala hūṃ phaṭ! This is the second root mantra.
O hūṃ phaṭ! This is the third root mantra.
HŪṂ: the heart mantra. Ā: the second heart mantra. HA: the third heart mantra.

O Hrā Hrī Hrau! O you of fierce form! Tear asunder! Tear asunder! Rend! Rend! Quiver! Quiver! Spread abroad! Spread abroad! Strike! Strike! Devour! Devour! Bind! Bind! Render unconscious! Render unconscious! [Strike] all enemies!
Bind the mouths! Bind, bind! Terrify, terrify all the ḍākinīs, grahas, bhūtas, piśācas, and yakṣas! Kill, kill! Slay, slay! O Rurucaṇḍaruk, protect Devadatta! Caṇḍamahāsena!
All [beings] command: O Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, hūṃ phaṭ!
The garland mantra: Homage to all the Tathāgatas who fulfill all aspirations! Sarvathācalakānanā naṭṭa 2 moṭṭa 2 saṭṭa 2 tuṭṭa 2 tiṣṭha 2 āviśa 2 ĀḤ!
O great minister-child! Shake, shake! Chew, chew! Eat, eat! Slay the obstacles, slay! Devour the wicked, devour! Perform all [tasks], perform! *Kiri*, *kiri*!
O Great Poisonous Vajra, *phaṭ*! *Hūṃ* three times! You who possess the whirlpools of triple-folded waves!
HŪṂ 3 | Acala-ceṭa PHAṬ SPHĀṬAYA 2 HŪṂ 2 ASAMANTIKE TRĀṬ | Mahābala SĀṬAYA SAMĀNĀYA TRĀ MĀ HĀ | May the worlds be purified! May the Vajrin be pleased! Homage to those of unimpeded power!
Jvālaya trāṭ asaha namaḥ svāhā. This is the second garland mantra.
Namaḥ sarvāśāparipūrakebhyaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyaḥ sarvathā trāṭ amoghacaṇḍamahāroṣaṇa sphoṭaya 2 hūṃ.
*Bhramaya 2 trāṭ mohaya*. This is the third garland mantra (*mālāmantra*).
These are the general mantras of the five immovable ones (*pañcācala*). As for the specific mantras:
*Oṃ kṛṣṇācala hūṃ phaṭ*; *Oṃ śvetācala hūṃ phaṭ*.
O Pītācala hūṃ phaṭ! O Raktācala hūṃ phaṭ! O Syāmācala hūṃ phaṭ!
These are the general mantras of the goddesses. O Vajrayoginī!
HŪṂ PHAṬ. This is the root mantra. O PRAJÑĀPĀRAMITE HŪṂ PHAṬ. This is the second root mantra. O VAUHERI HŪṂ PHAṬ.
This is the third root mantra.
O Picu, increase wisdom! Blaze up, increase intelligence! Be firm, increase the intellect! Svāhā! This is the garland mantra (mālāmantra).
The specific mantras are as follows: Oṃ dveṣavajri hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ mohavajri hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ piśunavajri hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ rāgavajri hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ īrṣyāvajri hūṃ phaṭ.

This is the general mantra for the bali offering: Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, Śrī Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, the terrifier of gods, asuras, and humans, the destroyer of the entire force of Māras, whose head is adorned with a jeweled crown.
Accept this offering! Destroy all my obstacles!
Ward off the four Māras! Terrify! Confound! Bind! Split! Destroy! Burn! Dry up! Cut! Break!
Reduce to ashes those wicked beings who harbor hostile thoughts toward me!
Phaṭ 2 svāhā!
Thus ends the fifth chapter on mantras in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekalavīra. ||5||
Then the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, having firmly embraced the Blessed One and performed the friction of the lotus against the vajra, spoke.
"What kind of meditation is there through the yoga of the completion stage?
For the benefit of the yoginīs, please make fruitful that which has been asked."
Then the Blessed One said:
The yogi established in the yoga of the completion stage, devoted solely to yoga,
should meditate upon my form with a one-pointed mind day and night.
He should imagine his own wife to be completely filled with your form,
so that by means of intense and excessive union, she reaches a state of complete dissolution.
Mothers, daughters, sisters, nieces,
and all other female relatives, as well as Dombī women, Brāhmaṇīs, Caṇḍālīs, actresses, washerwomen, and courtesans— [all these are to be honored].
Likewise, there is the Vratini, the Yogini, and again the Kapālini.
And as for others, one should serve them according to the proper method— women well-established in female form as they are encountered— so that no breach occurs.
But if there is a breach, Caṇḍaroṣaṇa becomes enraged and slays the practitioner;
he casts him into the Avīci hell and terrifies him with a sword-noose.
In this world there would be no success, nor likewise in the next world;
therefore, it must be kept strictly secret and never made public.
Like the mantra of a ḍākinī, this sādhana of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa is to be kept secret;
it has been spoken by me, the Buddha, for the sake of those who desire the ultimate.
Having taken those women, who were pleasing to her own heart and desirable, to a secluded place that was agreeable to the mind and free from all disturbances;
"I am the Buddha, immovable and perfected; Prajñāpāramitā is my beloved.
Thus the wise one should meditate upon his own true nature with a firm mind.
Having made the hermitage solitary and subsisting on whatever food is obtained,
one should meditate intensely through the union of the two pairs with one another.
Having brought the woman face-to-face and seated her before him,
he should gaze intently at one another with both of them, out of mutual passion.
Then, meditating on the bliss of the vision, he should remain with a one-pointed mind;
by her, right there, words that produce the stimulation of bliss should be spoken.
"You are my son, you are my husband; you are considered by me to be my brother and my father.
I am your mother, your wife, your sister, and your sister’s daughter."
"By seven men you were my slave, my field-hand and servant;
you were bought by me for a cowrie-shell, and I am considered your mistress."
With his palms joined together in deep reverence, he fell at her feet.
In that situation, one should speak such words as are supremely inspiring and conducive to happiness:
"You are my mother and father; you are my wife and my sister."
You are my sister’s son and my wife, and you are my own sister;
I am your servant in every way, devoted with intense loyalty.
"Look at me with compassion, O Mother, with glances of affectionate love.
Then she embraced the man and kissed him again and again.
She offers the three-syllable mantra at his head; she places the honey of the mouth's flavor in his mouth;
she causes him to suck the lotus and displays the playfulness of her eyes to him.
Having applied ointment to her face, one should press her heart with one's own breast;
gazing face-to-face at her face, one should place the nails upon the abode of her mind.
He should speak these words to him: "O Vairocana, eat such food as this! O son, drink the water of Akṣobhya and become a slave to your father."
Your mistress, my mother, who belongs to the royal court, has also said:
"O child, go constantly to my feet for refuge."
Since you have attained worthlessness despite being reared by me, be grateful, my child; give me back the happiness born of the thunderbolt.
Behold the three-petaled lotus adorned with filaments in its center;
oh, how the field of Sukhāvatī is graced by the Buddha Amitābha!
Having pierced me— who am passionless, a giver of happiness, peaceful, and free from all conceptual constructions—
with her outstretched hand, she whose mind was overwhelmed by passion [departed].
Placing both feet upon the shoulder, gaze at me from below and above;
then, having visualized a throbbing vajra, cause it to enter the central aperture of the lotus.
Bestow upon me a thousand *dhāpa*, a hundred thousand, ten million, or even a billion [of flowers],
within my three-petaled lotus provided with a wick of incense.
Having cast your own vajra there, worship the mind with bliss:
"O Vāyu, O Vāyu, the unsurpassed essence of essences within my beautiful lotus!"
With a single-pointed mind, one should meditate on her as she speaks thus: "O Buddhas, with the tip of the vajra, [I shall bind] you who are red like the bandhūka flower," while remaining motionless.
One should cultivate that bliss arising from it, remaining steady through intense concentration of mind.
O beloved, if she should give a reply, do not delay for even a moment.
As long as I contemplate for even a moment the form of a woman’s body,
I realize that she alone is the auspicious Mother of the three worlds, the bestower of true happiness.
Those talkative ones established in evil deeds who revile here out of malice,
they [fall] by that very act into a hell difficult to traverse.
In the Raudra hell, they are always suffering;
with bodies burned by many fires, they remain there crying out for three kalpas.
However, the quality that must be spoken of in women is their embracing of all beings;
whether it be compassion or protection, it is firmly established in the hearts of women.
Let alone one's own kin, she even nourishes strangers by means of begging;
if she is such as this, it cannot be otherwise.
The woman is Vajrayoginī.
Let alone seeing her or even touching her;
by the mere remembrance of her, happiness is obtained instantly.
The five objects of the senses themselves abide in women with divine forms;
having married them, men enjoy happiness.
Therefore, O Mother, who are free from faults, adorned with all excellent qualities,
meritorious, most meritorious, and supremely auspicious, grant me your grace.
Then, seeing them tightly [pressed], the yogi should bite his own lip with his teeth while making the sound "śītkāra"; and she too should become naked.
One should perform the Sukhodaya-bandha, the Dolacālana-bandha,
the Jānugraha-bandha, and also the Ūrumardana-bandha.
The Pādacālanabandha, the Bandha, the Bhūmicāpita-bandha,
the Samadantaka-bandha, and the bandha known as Citra.
The Bhramarī-jāla-bandha, the Yantrārūḍhordhvapadaka,
likewise the Kūrma-bandha, and the Sarvatobhadra.
There, in the middle of the cross-legged posture, one should place a woman in a squatting position and join her pair of arms firmly to one's own shoulders.
His own pair of arms, having emerged from between her armpits and cast the thunderbolt into the lotus, is known as the "Arising of the Joy of Bondage."
With the two hands joined together in a braid-like lock (veṇībandha), one should slightly move both of them; this is known as the "swinging movement" (dolacālana).
Placing her two knees against one's own chest in a hollowed embrace,
this bond is called *jānukagraha*, formed by the application of hands that move like a swing.
One should place her two soles upon the roots of one's own thighs;
through this placement which brings about the arising of bliss, this is the "thigh-crushing" (ūrumardana) bond.
Indeed, by placing the hands on her soles, navel, heart, and both sides,
this is the "Foot-Moving" (pādacālana) bind.
Having placed her two buttocks upon the ground within the hollow of her lap,
this "earth-pressed" (bhūmicāpita) bond is formed through the application of the sukha-udayakara mudrā.
Having established them in the squatting posture (utkuṭaka), one should extend both feet;
this is known as the Samadantaka bond, and one should likewise extend each foot individually.
Having placed the pair of her feet in a curved position, one should apply them to the left;
likewise on the right and facing forward, one should then touch the back with the heart.
One should perform the massaging of the hands and other limbs; this binding is known as Citra.
Having again brought about the arising of comfort, one should cause her to lie on her back.
With his left hand alone, he should place a vajra upon her lotus;
grasping the base of her knees, he should join his elbows upward.
When their hands are entwined like braids, it is known as the *bhramarī-jāla*;
having placed her pair of feet upon his own shoulders, he should hold them firmly.
This binding, indeed, is mounted upon a machine through the application of penetration and possession;
her left foot is placed on his shoulder, and the right [foot] at the root of her left thigh.

With one foot placed upon the shoulder of the other side and the other foot at the root of the opposite thigh— with the feet thus positioned upwards— this is indeed the Aya-bandha, which provides true comfort and destroys suffering.
One should place the soles of her feet evenly against the middle of one's chest;
pressing the knees with both arms is declared to be the tortoise-bind (kūrmabandha).
One should apply [the syllables] to her soles, eyes, ears, and head;
this binding is called Sarvatobhadra, which bestows all desires and happiness.
One should perform all manner of various wonders until reaching the limit of the multicolored;
then, by means of the Caṇḍaroṣaṇa yoga, one should press [the victim] firmly with the chest.
And he should kiss her face again and again as much as he desires,
raising her face and looking at her while speaking whatever words he wishes.
One should suck her tongue and drink the saliva arising from her mouth;
one should eat the dental plaque smeared upon it and contemplate the bliss [therein].
One should slightly press the teeth and tongue while the lips are closed;
with the tongue, one should cleanse the nostril openings and the corners of the eyes.
One should consume the filth produced from the teeth and the armpits, as well as everything else [from the body]:
the brain, the eyes, the throat, the ears, the sides, the armpits, the hands, and the breasts.
Having kissed her, one should apply the nails; leaving the two eyes of the woman, one should rub with the hand, then suck and bite the *cuñcu*.
Having herself turned it upward, O one with a beautiful belly, she should kiss it;
right here he stood before, remembering again and again, over and over.
Touching the lotus with his hand while saying, "O Vāyusundarī," he should give her a kiss on the nail,
having drawn it away with his hand so that she may look at him.
Having smelled her scent, he should cleanse that opening with his tongue, thinking:
"I have entered through this many times, and I have emerged as well countless times."
One whose nose is straight should utter such words on this path;
for this alone shall be the path to the sixfold goal through the yoga of knowledge.
Through the application of knowledge, however, there arises the accomplishment of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa;
then, one should [offer] white or red lotuses that have been made into objects of pleasure.
And he should repeatedly devour her face while gazing upon it;
making his nails like claws on her thighs, he should massage her feet like a slave.
One should place the three syllables on the head and the *laghumuṣṭika* at the center of the heart;
thereafter, the concentrated yogi should perform other various bindings.
There, the meditator, with a mind focused solely on bliss, should emit [the seed] at will;
or, with a mind focused solely on bliss, he may not emit it at all, according to his desire.
When it has flowed, one should lick the lotus by means of prostrating with the knees;
one should consume the semen and blood from the lotus with the tongue.
By means of the nose and the application of a tube, one should drink for the sake of increasing capacity;
having cleansed the lotus with the tongue and aroused wisdom, one should kiss it.
Thereafter, having embraced her, he should eat fish and meat;
he may drink milk or wine again for the sake of increasing his passion.
When that fatigue has subsided, one should then desire [the practice] through means such as pleasure;
then, once again, one should begin the pairs in mutual alternation according to the previous sequence.
And by means of this yoga of practice, the knower of yoga attains great bliss and assumes the state of Caṇḍaroṣa in this very life.
For the sake of bestowing accomplishment upon those possessed of passion, I have revealed this yoga:
having placed the right leg playfully upon the left calf.
This celebrated sattvaparyaṅka posture bestows all desires and happiness;
it is formed by placing the left leg gracefully upon the right thigh.
This celebrated lotus posture (padmaparyaṅka) bestows all desires and happiness;
having assumed the lotus posture, one should place the left leg upward.
The vajraparyaṅka posture is defined as resting the left leg playfully upon the ground with the sole of the foot placed flat,
facing forward and extended straight.

This is to be known as the bestower of all desires; it is performed by squatting on the ground, placing the soles of the feet upon the ground with the knees wide apart and the thighs held horizontally and very far apart.
This is to be known as the Ardhacandrāsana (Half-moon posture), which bestows sensual pleasure;
here, the pair of knees is placed obliquely on the ground with a cushion between the ankles.
Having performed this bow posture (dhanvāsana), which bestows divine sensual pleasures,
one should likewise assume the lotus posture (sattvaparyaṅka) or the vajra posture (vajraparyaṅka).
The utkūṭaka, the ardhacandra, and the dhanvāsana are considered [variations of this];
women seated in the ardhacandrāsana position, placed closely together.
Having fallen down, one should lick it while holding the lotus with the three syllables of the *sulakṣa*;
then, assuming the bow-posture, one should place one's own face within its anus.
Having caused her anus to fall away, one should lick it with the tongue and also with the nose;
then, through the yoga of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa, one should meditate upon the bliss arising from that.
Then the yogi becomes liberated, free from all conceptual constructions;
having made the mind devoid of passion, he should desire through the measure.
Through attachment one obtains merit; through detachment, evil is obtained.
There is no sin greater than detachment, nor is there any merit greater than happiness.
And therefore, being composed, one should direct the mind toward the happiness born of desire.
Then the Blessed Lady, her heart filled with joy, having paid homage to and prostrated before the Blessed One, spoke thus.
O Blessed One, is this means of accomplishment intended for humans alone, or for others as well?
The Blessed One said:
"Those beings who are devoted here, dwelling in all directions—
gods, asuras, humans, and nāgas— they too shall attain accomplishment as practitioners."
Then, having heard this, Maheśvara and the other gods took Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Śacī, Rati, and the other goddesses and began to contemplate them. At that very moment, all of them— just then—
In that very moment, having attained the state of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa, they wander upon the surface of the earth. Therein, Maheśvara is perfected as Vajraśakra; Vāsudeva as Vajranārāyaṇa; and Devendra—
As Vajrapāṇi; as Kāmadeva, as Vajrānaṅga—headed by these, sons of the gods equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā attained accomplishment.
Endowed with the five qualities of sensual pleasure, they act for the benefit of all sentient beings;
assuming various forms, all these victorious ones are beings who manifest through illusion.
Just as a lotus born from the mud is not defiled by the faults of the mud,
so too those born from the way of passion are not defiled by faults.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Perfected Yoga, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekalavīra.
Then the Blessed One said: "For a living being engaged in sexual union, there would be great exhaustion;
O Lord, you ought to speak for the sake of that being’s rest."
The Blessed One said:
Having fully embraced the pleasure of women and suppressed [the senses] within his own direct perception,
he should eat fish and meat and drink wine with a concentrated mind.
One should first give women whatever food has been obtained— be it rice, milk, water, or other edibles— and then one may consume their leftovers.
One should eat continuously from her *ucchiṣṭayantra* (the vessel of her leavings),
and one should drink the water used for her ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) as well as the water used for washing her lotus-feet.
The observer of the vow, having washed his anus, should wash his mouth and other parts;
he should consume the vomit of that [cow], and he should also consume the *catuḥsama*.
One should drink water born from the source and consume morsels of spittle;
just as a tree, having received the letter 'sa', becomes abundant with fruit.
In the same way, by the enjoyment of impurity, a human being would have the excellent fruit of happiness;
for that embodied soul, there would be neither old age, nor disease, nor death.
He who serves the impure, even if he is devoid of yoga, attains success;
whether it be edible or inedible, one should not form any conceptual distinctions whatsoever.
The knower of Yoga does not conceptualize what should or should not be done, nor what may or may not be approached;
he does not conceive of merit or sin, nor of heaven or liberation.
The yogi, concentrated and intent on meditation, should remain as the single embodiment of innate bliss;
indeed, such a yogi becomes truly joined with yoga if he is devoted to this cultivation.
If one who maintains the ego through the singular yoga of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa were to kill even a hundred Brahmins, he is not tainted by sins.
Therefore, O Lord, one should meditate upon Caṇḍaroṣaṇa in such a manner that by it sentient beings who have committed terrible deeds may go to hell.
By that very means, together with its method, they attain liberation without a doubt;
for it is held that all sin and merit are preceded by the mind.

Just as poison, when transformed by the mind through differences in its conceptual form, mode of movement, location, and so forth, leads to the destruction of life even when consumed after being consecrated with mantras; [so too is the nature of mental objects].
Having thus performed the consecration with that very [mantra], happiness and longevity increase.
Then, at that moment, the supreme goddess Prajñāpāramitā [appeared].
With a skull-bowl held in her hand, and displaying the mudrā of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa,
the greatly enraged Vajracaṇḍī should speak these supreme words.
Having meditated upon my form and conceived the supreme ego-sense,
even if she were to kill a hundred Brahmins, she would not be tainted by sins.
Assuming my form with a mind focused solely on great wrath,
the Yoginī may kill fish and birds, yet she is not defiled.
For women are generally pitiless, fickle, wrathful, intent on killing, and preoccupied with their own interests; it is for their sake that this [work] has been revealed.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the Satisfying of the Body, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekalavīra*.
Then the Blessed One, having prostrated with the five-pointed salutation to the Blessed Lady, spoke.
O beloved, how indeed is your form to be known by a yogi?
And by which yogi will the Blessed Lady be propitiated?
Then the Blessed One said:
For whatever female form is seen in the world, throughout the three realms, that is my own form appearing in families, high and low.
A goddess, an asura woman, a yakṣiṇī, and likewise a rākṣasī;
a nāginī, a daughter of a bhūtinī, a kinnarī, and likewise a human woman.
A Gandharvī, a Nārakī, a maiden of the animal realm, and a Pretikā;
a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriṇī, a Vaiśyā, and a Śūdrā—these are the extremely extensive [categories].
Kāyasthī, Rājaputrī, Śiṣṭinī,
Karauttinī, Vaṇijinī, Vāriṇī, Veśyā, Tariṇī, and Carmakāriṇī.
The woman of the Kula, the woman of the Hunter, the Dombī, the Cāṇḍālī, and likewise the Śavarī;
the washerwoman, the liquor-seller, the woman of the perfumer, and the laborer.
A weaver’s wife, an actress, a maker of garlands,
a goldsmith, a fisherwoman, a basket-maker, a maker of earthen vessels, and a garland-maker— these are the [eight].
Kāpālinī, Śaṅkhinī, Varuḍinī,
Kemālinī, Gopālī, Kāṇḍakārī, Kocinī, and Śilākuṭī.
The mother-in-law, the female hairdresser, and those encompassed by all castes—
the mother, the sister, the wife, and my own niece.
The younger sister, the own sister, and any woman of all castes;
likewise the female ascetic, the female yoginī, the widow, and the female practitioner of austerities.
Thus, many such women,
all possessing forms identical to mine, remain established in their own respective natures for the sake of all sentient beings.
By means of kissing, embracing, and so forth, according to their availability,
these very women are served by the yogin through the union of the vajra and the lotus.
But women, when served by one who desires the welfare of all beings, grant accomplishment in a mere instant; therefore, one should serve women.
Women are heaven; women are dharma; women alone are supreme austerity;
women are awakening; women are the Saṅgha; women are the Perfection of Wisdom.
They are conceptualized through the distinctions of five colors and designated by different names:
the woman who is blue in color is proclaimed as Dveṣavajrī.
The woman who is white and fair is considered to be Mohavajrī;
the woman who is yellow in color is the goddess Piśunavajrikā.
The woman who is red and fair is proclaimed as Rāgavajrī;
the woman who is dark-complexioned is called Īrṣyāvajrī.
The one and only Blessed Lady Prajñā is established in five forms:
through flowers, incense, and so forth; through garments; and through the beauty of verses and prose as her limbs.
Through conversation and salutations, through holding joined palms in reverence,
through sight and touch, and even through remembrance or by acting upon their words;
One should constantly worship Vajrayoginī with kisses and embraces;
when physically able, this should be performed with the body, and when unable, with speech and mind.
Therefore she said: "When worshipped and satisfied, I grant all accomplishments;
having abandoned the form of the bodies of all women, I do not become anyone else."
"Having abandoned the worship of women, there shall be no other worship for me;
by this propitiation, I shall be pleased for the sake of the practitioner's success."
Always and everywhere, she is eternally within the range of his vision;
having meditated upon her as my own self in every form, one should desire one's own wife.
Through the union of the vajra and the lotus, I am the bestower of enlightenment upon him;
therefore, he should be intent on propitiating me in every possible way.
Even if one should commit theft, or the killing of a living being,
or speak false words, or destroy an image and the like,
or consume what belongs to the Saṅgha, or the property of a stūpa belonging to another;
The yogi who is intent upon my worship is not defiled by sins.
One should crush lice with one's nail and kill even those residing on clothing;
by this very practice, the observer of the vow should propitiate Mā.
One should not fear sin or the miserable states such as the hells;
rather, one should fear the world, for its power cannot be overcome.
There is indeed no evil whatsoever, nor is there any merit whatsoever;
the establishment of evil and merit exists only for the sake of protecting the minds of worldly beings.
Since everything is mind-only and its duration lasts but a single moment,
who indeed goes to hell, and who truly goes to heaven?
Just as death from a disease is brought about by the poison of one's own imagination even in the absence of actual venom,
so too does one fall into a lower state despite the absence of [actual] sin;
likewise, through the thorough knowledge of reality, Nirvana is attained by the wise.
Nirvana, however, is of the nature of emptiness, like a lamp [extinguished] by the wind.
And upon its severance, he too shall suffer in hell and shall not attain the state of enlightenment;
therefore, renouncing everything, the practitioner of vows should worship me alone.
I grant Caṇḍasiddhi in a mere instant; of this there is no doubt.
Then the Blessed One spoke to the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā.
"What would be the form of the fierce one, and what is his accomplishment? The Blessed Lady said:
The Yoginīs who have been proclaimed according to the distinction of five colors—
their respective husbands likewise [correspond] by the distinction of five colors.
All these have been described by me as fierce yoginīs;
however, he who is the blue-colored husband is known as Nīlācala.
For that husband who is white-complexioned is known as Śvetācala;
and that husband who is yellow-colored is celebrated as Pītakācala.
For that husband who is red and white is called Rakta-acala;
and that husband who is dark-complexioned is known as Śyāmaka-acala.
He who is truly one alone becomes Caṇḍa, abiding in five forms;
this is declared to be Caṇḍa, and his perfection arises from steadfastness.
Abiding in a divine form as far as the limits of space,
Caṇḍī becomes accomplished just as Caṇḍasiddhi was described.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Essential Nature, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekalavīra*.
